raw_response:
Catalogue-only results for C02

These seven candidates were translated by an internal model. Each was discovered in an opened awesome list, then checked through primary project or documentation pages. Their application to pods is an inference, not a claim of deployment or demonstrated usefulness. No change to the privilege of the kubelet or container runtime is required by this translation.

1. Linux user namespaces: identity maps and namespace-owned capabilities
URL: https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/user_namespaces.7.html
Useful part: User namespaces provide the kernel mechanism for mapping workload UID/GID 0 to unprivileged host IDs while confining capabilities to resources owned by the workload's user namespace.
Application: Pod identity boundary and capability checks; use a pod-owned user namespace with appropriate ownership of its other namespaces.
Conditions: Shared-kernel vulnerabilities remain; file access depends on mapped identities, and namespace ownership matters. The opened manual is later evidence.
Timing: post_decision. Opened manual is Linux man-pages 6.19 dated 2026-02-08; the separately opened Red Hat article dated 2015-07-07 confirms earlier UID/GID-remapping availability, but does not backdate this manual.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

2. OCI runtime-spec Linux namespace and ID-mapping configuration
URL: https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec/blob/main/config-linux.md
Useful part: OCI's user namespace plus uidMappings and gidMappings fields provide an existing runtime-facing representation of container IDs, host IDs, and mapping sizes.
Application: Translate a pod's allocated ranges into container-runtime configuration; namespace paths can connect containers to an existing namespace.
Conditions: The orchestrator must allocate and manage nonoverlapping ranges; OCI leaves those policies outside this schema and cautions against changing referenced filesystem ownership.
Timing: unknown. Live main-branch specification opened; v1.0.2 content fetches were blocked and the release-year verification link denied access.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

3. Podman automatic UID/GID ranges and explicit rootful mappings
URL: https://docs.podman.io/en/v4.3/markdown/podman-run.1.html
Useful part: Podman's --userns=auto allocation of unique UID/GID ranges offers a concrete model for assigning disjoint host identities to workloads.
Application: Range allocation and mapping-size policy; the rootful mapping path is relevant without requiring an unprivileged kubelet or runtime.
Conditions: A subordinate-ID pool must be configured, volume ownership needs handling, and mappings cannot be set per container when joining a pod.
Timing: unknown. Official versioned v4.3 manual and current manual were opened; no dated release source establishing v4.3 availability by cutoff was verified.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

4. Sysbox user-namespace isolation and exclusive-mapping design
URL: https://github.com/nestybox/sysbox/blob/master/docs/user-guide/security.md
Useful part: Sysbox documents retaining root capabilities inside a container while translating both UID and GID ranges and offering exclusive ranges for cross-container isolation.
Application: Runtime enforcement, range exhaustion policy, and compatibility handling for mounted files.
Conditions: The opened guide assigns common mappings to CE and exclusive mappings to EE; exhaustion may reuse ranges unless configured to fail, and mounted files require ID-mapped mounts or shiftfs.
Timing: unknown. Live security guide opened; attempted v0.5.0 security-guide retrieval was blocked, so current details are not backdated.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

5. LXC unprivileged-container UID/GID mapping implementation
URL: https://github.com/lxc/lxc
Useful part: LXC provides a concrete implementation reference for paired UID/GID maps that make container root appear as an unprivileged identity on the host.
Application: Mapping setup, privileged helper boundaries, and compatibility restrictions for a container runtime.
Conditions: Its documented unprivileged-launch helpers do not require adopting a rootless kubelet; pod-wide coordination and disjoint allocation still need separate design.
Timing: unknown. Live README opened; no dated snapshot of these implementation details was verified.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

6. NsJail configurable UID/GID maps and capability retention
URL: https://github.com/google/nsjail
Useful part: NsJail combines explicit inside/outside UID and GID ranges with user namespaces, selected capability retention, and syscall filters as an inspectable confinement component.
Application: Prototype and reference implementation for mapping and capability setup around workload processes.
Conditions: It is a process-isolation tool rather than a pod runtime; allocation, namespace sharing, and lifecycle integration must be added.
Timing: unknown. Live README options and configuration example opened; no dated historical version verified.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/Friz-zy/awesome-linux-containers/blob/master/README.md

7. gVisor application-kernel isolation
URL: https://github.com/google/gvisor
Useful part: gVisor's userspace application kernel can reduce the host-kernel interface reachable by a workload as an additional approach to limiting escape impact.
Application: Alternative runtime boundary for incremental hardening against kernel or runtime vulnerabilities.
Conditions: It does not itself specify the requested pod UID/GID allocation policy; workload compatibility and performance would require evaluation.
Timing: unknown. Live project README opened; no dated source establishing the described version by cutoff was verified.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/veggiemonk/awesome-docker

Historical supporting reference: the catalogue-linked Red Hat article at https://rhelblog.redhat.com/2015/07/07/whats-next-for-containers-user-namespaces/ is dated July 7, 2015 and describes mapping container root and other users/groups to different host identities, including different mappings for separate containers. It establishes that mapping approach before the cutoff; it does not establish the dates of the current implementation details above.

Evidence limits: two potentially target-related search snippets appeared despite the catalogue-restricted query strings and were excluded. The current namespace manuals are dated 2026. The other live or insufficiently dated versioned pages remain date-unknown. No prohibited proposal document was opened.
